pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
> 🔤 **Strand 2 — Algebra**
Using letters and symbols to describe patterns, relationships and unknown quantities.

> 🎯 **Content standard** (B9.2.3)
- B9.2.3.1 — Demonstrate understanding of single variable linear inequalities with rational coefficients, including solving, verifying, comparing and graphing inequalities.

> 🎯 **In this chapter you will learn to:**
- solve linear inequalities with fractional (rational) coefficients
- illustrate solution sets on the number line and on the Cartesian plane
- solve real-life problems involving linear equations and inequalities

pages.title: Solving inequalities with rational coefficients
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Solve single variable linear inequalities with rational coefficients.
Curriculum indicator B9.2.3.1.1
> 🔑 **Key idea: Clearing fractions** — Multiply **every term** on both sides by the **LCM of the denominators** (a positive number, so the sign stays the same). Then solve as usual. Remember: multiplying or dividing by a **negative** number **reverses** the inequality sign.
## ✏️ Example 7.1
Solve: a) 2x + 7 > [[5/2]] b) [[4/5]] − x > [[1/5]] c) y − [[3/2]] < [[2/5]] d) [[1/2]](5x − 4) < x + [[11/2]]
**Solution**
a) Multiply by 2: 4x + 14 > 5 ⟹ 4x > −9 ⟹ **x > −**[[9/4]]
b) Multiply by 5: 4 − 5x > 1 ⟹ −5x > −3 ⟹ (÷ −5, reverse) **x <** [[3/5]]
c) Multiply by 10: 10y − 15 < 4 ⟹ 10y < 19 ⟹ **y <** [[19/10]]
d) Multiply by 2: 5x − 4 < 2x + 11 ⟹ 3x < 15 ⟹ **x < 5**
## ✏️ Example 7.2
Solve: a) [[x/3]] > x − [[4/5]] b) [[2x + 3/7]] ≤ x + 1 c) [[2/5]]x + [[1/2]] ≥ −[[3/2]] d) −[[2/3]]x + 3 ≥ 0
**Solution**
a) LCM 15: 5x > 15x − 12 ⟹ −10x > −12 ⟹ **x <** [[6/5]]
b) Multiply by 7: 2x + 3 ≤ 7x + 7 ⟹ −5x ≤ 4 ⟹ **x ≥ −**[[4/5]]
c) LCM 10: 4x + 5 ≥ −15 ⟹ 4x ≥ −20 ⟹ **x ≥ −5**
d) Multiply by 3: −2x + 9 ≥ 0 ⟹ −2x ≥ −9 ⟹ **x ≤** [[9/2]]
> 🎯 **BECE tip** **Verify** your solution by testing a value: in a), x = 0 should satisfy [[0/3]] > 0 − [[4/5]], i.e. 0 > −0.8 ✓, and x = 2 should not: [[2/3]] > [[6/5]] is false ✓.

pages.title: Illustrating solution sets
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Illustrate solution sets of linear inequalities on the number line.
Curriculum indicator B9.2.3.1.2
| **Inequality** | **In words** | **Number line** |
|---|---|---|
| x > a | x is greater than a | open circle at a, arrow to the right |
| x ≥ a | x is greater than or equal to a | closed circle at a, arrow to the right |
| x < a | x is less than a | open circle at a, arrow to the left |
| x ≤ a | x is less than or equal to a | closed circle at a, arrow to the left |
| a < x ≤ b | x is between a and b, including b | open circle at a, closed circle at b, segment between |
## ✏️ Example 7.3
Solve and graph on a number line: a) −3x − 8 > −26 b) 2x − 3 ≤ 19 c) −2 < x + 1 ≤ 4
**Solution**
a) −3x > −18 ⟹ **x < 6**
b) 2x ≤ 22 ⟹ **x ≤ 11**
c) Subtract 1 throughout: **−3 < x ≤ 3**
[[fig:m9-f12]]
Figure 7.1: Solution sets on number lines
## Inequalities on the Cartesian plane
On the Cartesian plane, x ≥ 4 is the **region** to the right of the vertical line x = 4 (including the line), and y < 1 is the region below the horizontal line y = 1 (not including the line). A **solid** boundary line is included; a **broken (dashed)** line is not. The region **not wanted** is usually shaded.
## ✏️ Example 7.4
Solve and show on the Cartesian plane: a) 2x ≥ 8 b) 5y + 3 < 6 + 2y c) [[7x/3]] < 7
**Solution**
a) **x ≥ 4** b) 3y < 3 ⟹ **y < 1** c) Multiply by 3: 7x < 21 ⟹ **x < 3**
[[fig:m9-f13]]
Figure 7.2: The wanted regions are left unshaded

pages.title: Real-life problems with equations and inequalities
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Solve real-life problems involving linear equations and inequalities.
Curriculum indicator B9.2.3.1.3
## ✏️ Example 7.5
A man has 260 m of fencing to put around a rectangular field 50 m wide. How long is the field?
**Solution**
Let the length be x m. Perimeter = 2(x + 50).
2(x + 50) = 260 ⟹ x + 50 = 130 ⟹ **x = 80 m**
## ✏️ Example 7.6
A man paid GH₵290 for 11 books. Some were geography books at GH₵30 each and the rest were history books at GH₵20 each. How many geography books did he buy?
**Solution**
Let x be the number of geography books; then 11 − x are history books.
30x + 20(11 − x) = 290 ⟹ 30x + 220 − 20x = 290 ⟹ 10x = 70 ⟹ **x = 7**
He bought 7 geography books (and 4 history books). Check: 210 + 80 = 290 ✓
## ✏️ Example 7.7
Two sides of a triangle are 6 cm and 8 cm. What are the possible lengths of the third side?
**Solution**
The sum of any two sides of a triangle is greater than the third side (the **triangle inequality**). Let the third side be x cm.
6 + 8 > x ⟹ x < 14
6 + x > 8 ⟹ x > 2
8 + x > 6 ⟹ x > −2 (always true for a length)
So **2 < x < 14**: the third side is between 2 cm and 14 cm.
## ✏️ Example 7.8
A student scored 70 and 76 in two tests. Students with an average of 80 or more in three tests are put in Grade A. What must she score in the third test to get Grade A?
**Solution**
Let the third score be s.
[[70 + 76 + s/3]] ≥ 80 ⟹ 146 + s ≥ 240 ⟹ **s ≥ 94**
She must score at least 94.

pages.title: Exercise 7.3
pages.body:
> ✏️ **Exercise 7.3** — try these on paper or in your head, then tap **Quick check** to see the answers.
1. The perimeter of a square is at most 48 cm. What are the possible side lengths?
2. Esi has GH₵200. She buys a bag for GH₵65 and some books at GH₵18 each. What is the greatest number of books she can buy?
3. A taxi charges GH₵8 plus GH₵3.50 per km. Kofi has GH₵50. What is the greatest whole number of kilometres he can travel?
4. The sum of three consecutive even numbers is less than 100. Find the largest possible numbers.
5. A rectangle's length is 4 cm more than its width. Its perimeter is at least 40 cm. What is the smallest possible width?

pages.title: Chapter 7 summary
pages.body:
- Clear fractions by multiplying every term by the LCM of the denominators.
- Reverse the sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number.
- Open circle / dashed line: not included; closed circle / solid line: included.
- Triangle inequality: any two sides together are longer than the third.
